qa_pairs.question: For SSH interoperability, if python-cryptography's ML-KEM API is stateful — i.e. you load an `MLKEM768DecapKey` and call `decap(ciphertext)` on it, with no serialization involved in `decap` itself — will the proposed API work given the desire not to expose expanded decapsulation keys as a serializable type? Specifically, SSH needs raw public-key bytes on the wire: for `mlkem768x25519-sha256`, SSH sends 1184 bytes of ML-KEM public key plus a 32-byte X25519 public key, concatenated and encoded as an SSH string in `MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT`; the server then calls `encaps()` on the PQ public key bytes and sends back the 1088-byte ciphertext plus 32 bytes of X25519 shared data in `MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY`; the client calls `decaps()` with its private key and the ciphertext to recover the shared secret. Since liboqs's `keypair()` output was exactly what SSH needed on the wire, do we need anything beyond raw encapsulation-key bytes, and is seed-only private-key handling going to be a problem for SSH?
qa_pairs.answer: The interoperability test succeeded between this ML-KEM support using BoringSSL and a prior liboqs-based implementation. `public_bytes_raw()` on the public key produced exactly the bytes SSH needed on the wire, and the ciphertext returned from `encap` was also correct; the 32-byte secret was exchanged successfully in both directions. There was no need to serialize private-key data, so operating only on the seed rather than an expanded key is not a problem for SSH.

title: Handle links and other safe content inside translations

qa_pairs.question: In Rails, how can translations safely handle interpolated HTML-safe content like links without forcing the translation key itself to know whether an interpolation contains HTML? For example, today I have to write either: ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or: ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` But `text_html` should not have to know whether `insert` contains HTML or not, and Rails already has `SafeBuffer`, so it seems like that information is being thrown away during translation. Given translations like: ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` I would like this to work: ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` and produce: ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ``` Is there a Rails-supported way to do this nicely, or should Rails/rails-i18n handle SafeBuffer-aware joining automatically?
qa_pairs.answer: A maintainer replied that they had just implemented their own version of this behavior and shared it as a gist, saying they would love for something like it to become part of Rails or rails-i18n. No built-in Rails solution or merged fix was provided in the thread.

title: remove prepare script using husky and deprecated husky set from npm package

qa_pairs.question:
While installing axios@1.9.0 as a transitive dependency in a monorepo, npm fails with:
```
npm error .git can't be found
npm error > axios@1.9.0 prepare:hooks
npm error > npx husky set .husky/commit-msg "npx commitlint --edit $1"
npm error husky - install command is DEPRECATED

```
The published package appears to include these scripts:
`"scripts": {
  "prepare": "husky install && npm run prepare:hooks",
  "prepare:hooks": "npx husky set .husky/commit-msg \"npx commitlint --edit $1\""
}`

This breaks consumer installs because it assumes a `.git` directory exists, uses deprecated Husky commands (`install`, `set`), and runs developer-only tooling during install. Can axios remove the `prepare` script from the published package or otherwise change the hook setup so axios 1.9.0 installs safely as a transitive dependency in monorepos/CI, for example by moving hook setup to a local-only `husky:init` script?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says they created PR #6944 to switch to `postinstall` with safely guarded Husky install scripts so installation will not fail when there is no `.git` directory. They also say they prefer to keep hook setup automatic for contributors instead of requiring a manual `husky:init` command.

qa_pairs.question: Express 4.x currently depends on `body-parser@1.20.3`, which includes a vulnerable `qs` version. Can Express 4.x update its `body-parser` dependency to `1.20.4` so that users who have a dependency chain like "a dependency using express, which is using body-parser, which is using qs" can get the newer transitive dependency when they run `npm install express@4` in an existing install?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says it may be worth changing the dependency because doing so would force `npm install express@4` in an existing installation to update dependencies, which users seem to have trouble with otherwise. They also clarify that `qs < 16.4.1` is not malicious, but vulnerable, and note that its exact status is complicated.

title: README beforeRedirect example bypasses follow-redirects credential-stripping protection

qa_pairs.answer: Yes — the maintainer agreed that the README example should include a protocol check before re-injecting credentials, e.g. checking that the redirect URL is still `https:` before setting auth. They also said the docs should add a security note explaining that `follow-redirects` intentionally strips credentials on HTTPS→HTTP downgrades and that `beforeRedirect` runs after that stripping, so blindly re-injecting credentials defeats the protection.

qa_pairs.question: In axios 1.7.2, requests for path-relative URLs are being processed as protocol-relative URLs, which appears to allow SSRF. Is there a patch for this issue?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says the issue is fixed in version 1.7.4.

Our scan reports CVE-2022-25883 (medium severity) in the transitive dependency semver-7.5.0.tgz under jsonwebtoken-9.0.0.tgz on the master branch. title: Stripe.PaymentIntent type is incompatible with stripe-js version of PaymentIntent

qa_pairs.question:
I'm creating a PaymentIntent on the server with stripe-node, then stripping fields before returning it to the client because the full server-side `Stripe.PaymentIntent` includes sensitive data like `metadata`. I originally tried to convert it into `@stripe/stripe-js`'s `PaymentIntent`, but the types are incompatible because server-side fields like `last_payment_error.payment_method.customer` can be expanded objects while client-side they cannot. For example, my reducer is:

```ts
import { PaymentIntent } from '@stripe/stripe-js'
import Stripe from 'stripe'

// pi parameter should be of Stripe.PaymentIntent type - the server side PaymentIntent type definition
// But Stripe.PaymentIntent is incompatible with @stripe/stripe-js version of PaymentIntent.
// The below code results in Typescript error.

function reduceStripePIToPublishableKeyPermissions(pi: Stripe.PaymentIntent): PaymentIntent {
    return {
        id: pi.id,
        amount: pi.amount,
        client_secret: pi.client_secret,
        currency: pi.currency,
        description: pi.description,
        last_payment_error: pi.last_payment_error,
        next_action: pi.next_action,
        payment_method: pi.payment_method,
        payment_method_types: pi.payment_method_types,
        receipt_email: pi.receipt_email,
        setup_future_usage: pi.setup_future_usage,
        shipping: pi.shipping,
        status: pi.status,
        object: pi.object,
        canceled_at: pi.canceled_at,
        cancellation_reason: pi.cancellation_reason,
        capture_method: pi.capture_method,
        confirmation_method: pi.confirmation_method,
        created: pi.created,
        livemode: pi.livemode
    }
}
```

For most frontend operations it now looks like the client may only need the `client_secret`, but I wanted to use the PaymentIntent as the single source of truth for displayed amount/currency so the UI matches what will be charged. In this case, is Stripe's preferred approach to pass only the `client_secret` from the server and let the client retrieve anything else from Stripe as needed? Also, is there any built-in redaction function in stripe-node for turning a server-side PaymentIntent into a safe client-side shape?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says there is no built-in redaction function in stripe-node, and they would not add one for now. They suggest that if you want to expose more than `client_secret`, you should send your own separate object from your server to your client with fields like amount and currency, rather than trying to reuse the full PaymentIntent type; retrieving the PaymentIntent with a publishable key server-side would be equivalent to doing it client-side after passing back the `client_secret`.

title: Vulnerable dependency version that is 12 years old: path-to-regexp

qa_pairs.question:
In Express 4.22.1 on all platforms with Node.js 22.x, `npm audit` reports a vulnerable dependency because Express pulls in `path-to-regexp`, and the installed version appears to be 12+ years old according to Snyk/npm metadata. The relevant references are:
- https://security.snyk.io/package/npm/path-to-regexp
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/path-to-regexp?activeTab=versions

Express 4.22.1 depends on `path-to-regexp`; why is `npm audit` flagging it as vulnerable/ancient, and what version should actually be installed for Express 4.22.1? If an older version is installed, what should I do?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says Express 4.22.1 specifies `path-to-regexp` as `~0.1.12`, which should currently resolve to `0.1.13`, released recently. They note Snyk shows `0.1.13` is not known to be affected by vulnerabilities, and that the “Published: 13 years ago” text refers to the package line, not that the current resolved release is outdated. If an older version is installed, they advise running `npm update path-to-regexp` or `npm audit fix`; a fresh install should also bring in `path-to-regexp@0.1.13`.
